rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The moderate temperature leaves room to probe temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Change only gradient duration to distinguish slope-sensitive overlaps from selectivity-limited pairs, especially the tight late triplet. This diagnostic run may incur a time penalty but will guide subsequent window trimming and temperature optimization.
The shallower gradient did not resolve the critical overlaps and exceeded the time target. Return to the faster gradient and test higher temperature for selectivity changes and shorter retention.

Test the shallower gradient at the temperature that gave the best score, looking for separation of the reordered early and late triplets. This isolates the slope response at 60 C before trimming the gradient window to recover time.

Raise the starting fraction and narrow the gradient window to retain a slope close to injection 4 while bringing the last peak below 10 minutes. This tests whether the early peaks tolerate the stronger start and whether the improved critical-pair separations persist.

Use an intermediate slope between injections 3 and 4 while preserving the weaker start that separated the early triplet better. The last peak should remain close to 10 minutes, allowing improved resolution without a substantial time penalty.

Probe the low-temperature selectivity branch using the same gradient as the current best method. Several close pairs change order or approach co-elution as temperature rises, so cooling may reveal a better separation pattern despite somewhat longer retention.

Test a stronger start with a shallower gradient to improve the late critical pairs while keeping the last peak near 10 minutes. This also checks whether the early triplet separates again beyond its observed order change, and quantifies the early-pair compression penalty.

Move beyond the early-triplet crossover seen at phi0 0.20 while further flattening the gradient to improve the late overlap. The preceding run leaves time headroom, but early-peak compression will determine whether this stronger start is worthwhile.

Keep the starting fraction below the early-peak compression limit and use the remaining time headroom for a shallower gradient. Relative to injection 8, this should improve the middle and late critical pairs while keeping the last peak near 10 minutes.

Test temperature selectivity at the best gradient window, focusing on the nearly co-eluting early pair. The weaker-start temperature results may not predict this reordered pattern, so this run measures whether improved early separation can outweigh losses in the late triplet.

Explore a substantially steeper gradient to test the alternative selectivity branch beyond the observed triplet order changes. This sacrifices some peak spacing but could separate the current overlaps in the opposite order while eliminating time penalties.

Refine between the two promising stronger-start methods: lowering phi1 from injection 5 should improve the late overlap, while phi0 0.15 avoids the near-co-elution at phi0 0.20. The predicted last-peak time remains below 10 minutes.

Test the low-temperature branch at the stronger starting fraction, where cooling has moved the early pair away from its crossover. A steeper gradient compensates for increased retention and should keep the last peak near 10 minutes.

Fine-tune the best method to a slightly shallower slope, using a narrower endpoint window to access a finer effective slope on the grid. The last peak is expected just under 10 minutes, with modest improvement in the remaining slope-sensitive overlaps.

Test whether cooling rescues the early and middle overlaps caused by the stronger start at phi0 0.25. A slope of about 0.043 per minute uses the retention headroom from injection 9 while targeting a last peak near 10 minutes.

Refine the promising phi0 0.25 branch at an intermediate temperature to balance early-triplet separation against the late overlap. A slightly shallower gradient should improve the middle and late pairs while the temperature increase keeps the last peak near 10 minutes.

Test an intermediate temperature at phi0 0.15, where cooling may improve both the first pair and the early triplet without the compression seen at phi0 0.25. The gradient slope is chosen to keep the last peak near 10 minutes while retaining useful late-pair separation.

Test the unmeasured starting fraction between the weak-start and stronger-start branches, with a slope expected to place the last peak near 10 minutes. This checks whether improved early-triplet selectivity can offset any loss in the first-pair separation.

Refine the promising stronger-start branch midway between injections 16 and 17. This slope-temperature combination should keep the last peak near 10 minutes while balancing losses across the early, middle, and late critical pairs.

Test a finer temperature balance at phi0 0.15: modest cooling may restore first-pair resolution and improve the early triplet's total contribution. The slope is chosen to place the last peak close to 10 minutes while preserving late-pair separation.

Refine the weak-start branch with a slightly shallower slope than injection 6, targeting a last peak at about 10 minutes. This should improve its three unresolved pairs without introducing the early-triplet compression of stronger starts.

Test the next shallower accessible slope near the best method to measure the tradeoff at the 10-minute boundary. The critical late pair should improve, but this run will establish whether that gain outweighs the small expected time penalty.

Test the remaining intermediate-temperature candidate on the stronger-start branch, using a shallower slope to bring the late pair closer to resolution. The temperature increase should offset the longer gradient and keep the last peak near 10 minutes.

Use the final injection to slightly flatten the promising injection 20 gradient, targeting its several partially resolved pairs simultaneously. This tests whether their combined resolution gain outweighs the small expected time penalty near the 10-minute boundary.
